newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Gujral says no change in Kashmir policy.
newsitem.headline: India's Gujral says no change in Kashmir policy.

text.p: Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral said on Monday India's policy on Kashmir had not changed and denied he had made and later withdrawn an offer for unconditional talks with separatists.
"No new policy statement has been made," Gujral told parliament in response to opposition charges after reports that he had made an offer for unconditional talks with separatists.
"I have always been willing to talk to the young boys who are our own children like in a family," he said.

Gujral made a stunning statement aimed at separatists during a trip on Saturday to Jammu and Kashmir, mainly Hindu India's only Moslem majority state. "I am willing to talk to them without any conditions," he said.
On Sunday he made an about-face, saying talks would not be held unless the militants waging a seven-year war against New Delhi laid down their arms.
"I strongly protest against the allegations that I say one thing in the morning and another in the evening," Gujral told the lower house, Lok Sabha, on Monday.
Gujral said his offer for talks was aimed at young men who he said were misled by separatist propaganda.
"During the speech I had said I was prepared to talk to all those young men who have been misled," he said.

"The same policies were followed even during the 13-day government of Atal Bihari Vajpayee," he said in response to criticism from members of Vajpayee's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Vajpayee, who was prime minister in the short-lived BJP government, said Gujral's statement had been publicised on state television, giving rise to doubts on the government's Kashmir policy.
"The manner in which the statement has been published and appeared on the television says a lot," Vajpayee said.

Gujral said there had been several skirmishes involving militants and Indian security forces along the Pakistan border for the past three or four months. He said his offer for talks was not aimed at militants trained across the border.
Police and hospitals say more than 20,000 people have been killed during the rebellion in Jammu and Kashmir, mainly Hindu India's only Moslem majority province.
India accuses Pakistan, which controls one-third of Kashmir, of arming Islamic militants in the Himalayan valley.
Pakistan, which has fought two wars with India over the region, denies the charge and says it only provides moral and diplomatic support to militants.
